en: This is the work of Maitreyanātha.
Oṃ, homage to the Protector Maitreya!
That which, through omniscience, leads the disciples seeking peace to tranquility;
that which, through the knowledge of the paths, accomplishes the welfare of the world for those who act for the benefit of beings;
and that through which the Sages, having attained union, declare this entire universe to be endowed with all aspects—[that is the Perfection of Wisdom].
I pay homage to that Buddha who possesses a multitude of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
The path to the knowledge of all aspects, which has been taught here by the Teacher,
the wise should behold as something not yet tasted by others.

Having established the meaning of the sūtras within mindfulness, the practice of the Dharma consisting of ten aspects is undertaken so that they may proceed with ease; this is the purpose of the undertaking.
The perfection of wisdom is proclaimed by means of eight categories:
omniscience in all its aspects, knowledge of the paths, and then omniscience.
Complete awakening in all its aspects, the summit, the gradual,
the awakening in a single moment, and the Dharma-body— these are your eight [forms].
The generation of the thought of enlightenment, instruction, the fourfold limb of penetration,
and the basis of practice, which has the dharmadhātu as its intrinsic nature.
The object of focus, the aim, the acts of donning armor and setting out,
the provisions together with the departure— these constitute the omniscience of all aspects belonging to the Sage.

The path of seeing, which possesses great benefits through its worldly and otherworldly virtues, consists of the acts of darkening and so forth, as well as the paths of the disciple and the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha].
Activity, resolute belief, and being praised, extolled, and lauded;
as well as the two unsurpassed mental orientations regarding dedication and sympathetic joy.
Accomplishment, ultimate purity—this is the path of cultivation for wise Bodhisattvas; thus is the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) proclaimed.
Through wisdom there is no abiding in existence; through compassion there is no dwelling in peace.
Without skillful means there is remoteness [from enlightenment]; with skillful means there is no remoteness.
The path of seeing for the Śrāvakas and others is held to be omniscience (sarvajñatā) when it consists of the discordant factors and their antidotes, the application, and its equality.

The aspects, along with their applications; the qualities and faults together with their characteristics; the stages conducive to liberation and penetration; the learner; and the irreversible assembly. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.12)
And the equality of existence and peace, as well as the unsurpassed purification of the field—
this is the complete awakening in all its aspects, together with skill in means.
Its sign, its increase, its firm rooting, and the stability of the mind;
these are the fourfold counteragents to the fourfold conceptual construction.
On each of the two paths known as seeing and cultivation,
there is the uninterrupted concentration, along with the errors.
The realization of the summit is threefold; that which is successive is tenfold;
and the realization in a single moment is fourfold by way of its characteristics.
The essential body, the body of enjoyment, and likewise the other, the emanation body— the Dharma-body, together with its activity, is thus proclaimed to be fourfold.
The production of the thought of enlightenment is the desire for perfect awakening for the sake of others;
it is explained both concisely and in detail according to the sūtras.
Through the earth, gold, the moon, and fire; through treasures, mines, and oceans;
through diamonds, mountains, medicinal herbs, and friends; and through the wish-fulfilling gem, the sun, and songs. // Abhs_1.19 //
And that [perfection] is of twenty-two kinds, consisting of the king, the treasury, the great road, vehicles, flowing water, the words of Ānanda, rivers, and clouds. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.20)
And [it consists of] practice regarding the truths, the three jewels beginning with the Buddha, non-attachment, lack of weariness, and the complete embracing of the path. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.21)
In the five eyes, in the six qualities of superknowledge,
and in the path of seeing as well as that called the path of cultivation— thus the instruction is tenfold in nature.

Those of dull and sharp faculties, those who have attained through faith and through vision, those who go from family to family, those with one interval, those who attain nirvāṇa in the intermediate state, those who attain it upon being reborn, those who attain it with effort, those who attain it without effort, and those who go to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.

The three types of leapers, those for whom existence is at its peak, those who have overcome attachment to the form realm, those who attain peace in this very life, the body-witnesses, and the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas]— these constitute twenty.

For the sake of the virtuous who, according to their respective natures, engage with the fourfold conceptualization through its objective support, its aspect, its causality, and its thorough grasping.
The superiority of the [levels of] heat and so forth—whether weak, medium, or intense—of the protecting Bodhisattva over the Śrāvakas who possess the sword is established. Abhs 1.26.
The objective support consists of impermanence and so forth, based upon the truths and having their form;
it is the negation of dogmatic adherence and the like, serving as the cause for attaining the three vehicles.

The coming and going, the departure and staying, and the ineffability of designation regarding form and so forth—these are their abiding in form and so on; by virtue of that [abiding], they lack intrinsic nature.
The mutual nature of those two is the non-establishment of their impermanence and so forth;
the emptiness of those [characteristics] of that nature is the mutual nature of these two.
Non-apprehension of phenomena is the non-contemplation of their signs and the investigation by means of wisdom through the non-perception of everything.
The absence of intrinsic nature in form and so forth is their having non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
their non-arising is their non-departure, and their purity is their signlessness.
Non-apprehension due to the non-appropriation of those signs is non-conceptuality;
its function is meditative concentration, its prediction, and the exhaustion of mentation.
The intrinsic nature of the three together and non-conceptuality regarding meditative concentration—
these constitute the levels conducive to penetration, categorized as weak, medium, and intense.
The conceptualization of the apprehended object is twofold, by way of the entity itself and its antidote;
each of these is further divided ninefold according to the categories of the mass of delusion and so forth.
The grasper is considered to be twofold, having as its basis both substantial entities and designations:
[the former] in the form of an independent self and so forth, and [the latter] by way of relying upon the aggregates and so on.

The absence of despondency of mind and so forth, the teaching on the lack of intrinsic nature and so forth, the abandonment of their opposites, and the complete embracing [of these qualities] in every way—[these constitute the perfection of wisdom]. Abhs 1.36.
Of the dharma of sixfold realization, of the abandonment of the opposites,
of the employment of those two, and of wisdom together with compassion.
The lineage (gotra) is said to be the foundation for the non-commonality with disciples, for the sequence of acting for the sake of others, and for the effortless operation of gnosis.
Because the dharma-sphere is indivisible, a distinction in lineage is not tenable;
however, that distinction is proclaimed on account of the distinction among the qualities to be contained within it.
The objective support consists of all phenomena; these, moreover, are the wholesome and so forth, those known as mundane attainments, and those considered supramundane.
Dharmas that are with outflows and without outflows, those that are conditioned and unconditioned,
those dharmas shared with disciples, and those that are unique to the Sage.

The objective of the Self-Existent Ones (the Buddhas) should be understood as consisting of three greatnesses: supremacy among all sentient beings, and the threefold [greatness] of resolve, abandonment, and realization. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.42)
The practice of donning the armor, which consists of each of those six types— beginning with generosity— included within every one of them, is as it has been explained by means of six sets of six.

In the formless realms, in giving and the other perfections, in the path, in loving-kindness and the like, in the application of the perception of objects, and in the purifications of the three spheres; 1.44.
In the summary, in the six superknowledges, and in the method of the knowledge of all aspects,
the practice of setting out is to be known as that which mounts upon the Mahāyāna.
Compassion, the sixfold set beginning with generosity, calm abiding together with insight,
the path of union, and skillfulness in means.
Knowledge, merit, the path, the dhāraṇīs, and the ten stages;
as well as the counteragent—these should be known as the sequence of the practice of the accumulations.
The first stage is attained through tenfold preparation:
[the cultivation of] intention, being a source of benefit, and equanimity toward all sentient beings. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.48)
Renunciation, service to friends, seeking the support of the true Dharma,
constant state of mind directed toward renunciation, and longing for the body of a Buddha.
The teaching of the Dharma is intended as the tenth statement, which is truth;
and this should be known as their preparatory purification, because of the non-apprehension of their intrinsic nature.
Ethical discipline, gratitude, patience, great joy, vast compassion,
reverence, service to the teacher, and eighthly, vigor in giving and the other perfections.
Insatiability regarding learning, giving that is free from worldly motives, the complete purification of the Buddha-field, and tirelessness in the midst of saṃsāra. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.52)
Moral shame and dread of blame—these five consist of the nature of reflection;
as well as forest-dwelling, having few desires, contentment, and the practice of the ascetic purifications and austerities.
Not abandoning the training, revulsion toward sensual desires, world-weariness, the relinquishing of all possessions, being free from dejection, and being without regard for one's own life.
Familiarity, stinginess regarding one's family, places that lead to social distraction, self-exaltation, and contempt for others— these are the ten unwholesome paths of action.
By abandoning pride, arrogance, error, doubt, and the endurance of afflictions, one attains these ten [qualities] on the fifth stage.
By means of fulfilling generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom,
he completely abandons those whose minds are characterized by longing for disciples or pratyekabuddhas, as well as fear.
Being entreated, he is not discouraged; even when asked to give away everything, he does not become dejected.
Though emaciated, he does not reject those who seek his help; thus he attains the sixth stage.

The grasping at a self and a sentient being, the views of annihilation and permanence regarding the living soul and the person, and [the grasping] at signs and causes within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.59)
Establishment in the three realms, attachment, and a mind that is cowed; likewise, adherence to views regarding the Three Jewels and the precepts.
He for whom the twenty stains— consisting of disputes regarding emptiness and opposition to it—
are severed, reaches the seventh stage.
The knowledge of the three gates of liberation, the purity of the three spheres,
compassion without conceit, and the knowledge of the single principle of the equality of all phenomena.
The knowledge of receptivity to non-arising, the grasping of all phenomena as one,
the eradication of conceptual construction, and the abandonment of perceptions, views, and afflictions.
The settling of calm abiding, skill in insight,
the taming of the mind, and knowledge that is unimpeded everywhere.
The absence of attachment, moving at will to other fields simultaneously, and the perception of one’s own self-nature everywhere—these constitute the twenty [qualities]. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.65)
The knowledge of the minds of all beings, the play of the superknowledges, purity, the accomplishment of the Buddha-field, and the service to and examination of the Buddhas; Abhs_1.66 //
Sensory cognition, the purification of the Buddha-field, abiding like an illusion,
and the intentional taking up of existence— this activity is declared to be eightfold.
The infinite aspirations, the knowledge of the languages of gods and others, eloquence like a flowing river, and the supreme descent into the womb; Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.68.
And the excellence of lineage, caste, clan, retinue, and birth;
of the renunciation, the tree of enlightenment, and the abundance of the perfections.
Having transcended the nine stages, one is established on the Buddha-stage;
that knowledge by which this is known is to be understood as the tenth bodhisattva stage.
The antidote should be known as eightfold on the paths of seeing and cultivation,
for the sake of pacifying the eight conceptualizations of the grasped and the grasper.
Departure consists in the summary, in equanimity, in the absence of effort for the sake of sentient beings, and in the ultimate departure; departure has the characteristic of attainment.
And the departure into the knowledge of all aspects, which has the path as its domain;
this eightfold nature is to be known as the practice of departure. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.73)
The first chapter, on the Knowledge of All Aspects, in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, a treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

The dimming of the gods by its rays, its fitness for the [bodhisattvas], its restricted object, its pervasiveness, its intrinsic nature, and its activity—[these are the characteristics of light]. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 2.1)
In the system of the knowledge of the paths, this path of the śrāvakas is to be known through the non-apprehension of the aspects of the four noble truths.

Because the aggregates, such as form, are empty, and because there is no differentiation among the types of emptiness, the "heat" stage is attained; the "summit" stage is considered to consist in the non-apprehension of those [aggregates].
The patiences [are taught] by way of negating the abiding in the application of permanence and so forth regarding those [dharmas];
starting from the ten stages, there is the teaching on the extensive abidings.
It is declared that [the stage] consisting of the supreme mundane dharmas belongs to the path of the noble śrāvakas;
for what reason? Because the Buddha, having awakened, does not perceive [any] phenomena.
The futility of instruction by others due to their self-awakening,
and the profundity of their knowledge— these are declared of the Pratyekabuddhas (Khaḍgas).
For whatever purpose, wherever, and in whatever manner one listens to [the Dharma],
that very purpose becomes renowned for each of them accordingly, even if it be a word of ill repute.

The summary of the rhinoceros-like path (khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa-mārga) should be understood through the abandonment of the conceptualization of the object to be grasped, the non-abandonment of the grasper, and its basis. *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* 2.8.

The form of indicating the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without contradicting conventional designation is characterized by the stages of "Heat" (uṣmagata) and "Summits" (mūrdhagata), which are distinguished by the non-abandonment of form and so forth.

Patience consists in the non-appropriation of form and so forth by means of [the contemplations on] internal emptiness and the like; the state of supreme mundane dharmas consists in the aspects of the non-arising of form and so forth.
Through the four moments of patience and knowledge regarding each truth,
this path of seeing within the knowledge of the paths is said to be accompanied by its benefits.
Because there is no relationship of container and contained between suchness and the Buddha, they are not admitted as being mutually interchangeable;
that is their greatness and their immeasurability.

The absence of any limit to the measure [of merit], the determination of form and so forth, and, while abiding in that state, the non-abandonment of grace and so forth upon attaining Buddhahood. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 2.13)
The attainment of friendliness and so forth, the realization of emptiness, the embracing of buddhahood,
the purification of everything, and the destruction of all mental anguish and diseases.

The tranquility of grasping at nirvāṇa, the protection [of beings] by the Buddhas, and so forth—beginning with non-killing—[are taught] in the method of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā). (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 2.15)

Establishing beings in that which one has established oneself in, and the dedication of giving and so forth toward perfect enlightenment—these are the moments of the knowledge of the path (mārgajñatā). Abhs_2.16 //
Complete self-mastery is the name for the total conquest of the afflictions;
it is the state of being invincible to adversaries, awakening, and the worthiness of being honored as a support.

Resolve should be known as threefold: for one's own benefit, for the benefit of both oneself and others, and for the benefit of others alone; and each of these is further considered to be of three kinds.
It is weak, medium, and intense, according to the divisions of weak-weak and so forth;
since each of these is again threefold, it is thus considered to be twenty-sevenfold.
Praise, exultation, and commendation regarding the perfection of wisdom are held to consist of three sets of nine degrees of resolute conviction.
Its excellence is its transformation, which is its supreme activity;
it has the form of non-apprehension and is characterized by the absence of error.
It is secluded, its objective range being the recollection of the nature of the flood of a Buddha’s merit;
it possesses skillful means, is signless, and is approved by the Buddhas.
Furthermore, the transformation that does not enter into the three realms is of another threefold kind—
mild, middling, and intense— consisting in the arising of great merit.
The cultivation of the mental attention consisting of rejoicing in the roots of virtue through both skillful means and non-apprehension is prescribed here. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 2.24)

Its intrinsic nature is excellence; it consists in the non-constructive activity regarding all things, the non-apprehension of phenomena, and the dedication [of merit] for the sake of the great purpose.

Service to the Buddha in the form of giving and so forth, as well as skillfulness—these are the causes for resolute conviction here; [the following] are the causes for the ruin of the Dharma. *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* 2.26.
Lack of conviction in the profound nature of phenomena due to the influence of Māra,
attachment to the aggregates and so forth, and being under the sway of evil friends.
The purity of the fruit is indeed the purity of form and so forth; since there is no distinction between these two, they are inseparable—thus is purity proclaimed. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 2.28)

Purification through the abandonment of the three paths—of afflictions, of the knowable, and of both—is ultimate for the disciples, the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas], and the sons of the Victor; however, for the Buddha, it is absolute in every respect.
The path beginning with the "mild-mild" [grade] constitutes purification across the nine stages,
by virtue of being the antidote to the defilements beginning with the "intense-intense."
The equality of the mind and its object is intended as the antidote to the three realms;
this is established by way of avoiding that [dualistic conception] regarding the path.
The second chapter, on the Knowledge of the Path, in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, a treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
It does not abide on the near shore, nor on the far shore, nor in between the two;
because of the knowledge of the equality of the paths, it is considered the perfection of wisdom.
By means of what is not a skillful method, she is far away due to the apprehension of signs;
by skill in means, her correct proximity is proclaimed.
Regarding the emptiness of the aggregates such as form, regarding phenomena belonging to the three times,
and regarding the factors conducive to awakening such as generosity— conceiving of them as "practice" constitutes an adverse state.

Absence of egoism regarding giving and the like, enjoining others to those same practices, and the negation of attachment to millions of objects—this is subtle attachment toward the Victors and so forth. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 3.4)

"That profundity arises from the very nature of the discernment of the path of phenomena"—thus, knowledge of the single nature of all phenomena is the abandonment of attachment. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 3.5)
By means of the negation of being seen and so forth, its difficulty to comprehend is proclaimed;
because it is not cognized through forms and the like, its inconceivability is asserted.

Having established it thus, this exhaustive classification of the discordant factors and their antidotes should indeed be understood as it has been described in the system of omniscience. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 3.7)
Regarding form and so forth, their impermanence and so forth, their non-filling and filling,
and the non-attachment to them—
therein lies the application of the practice through negation. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 3.8)
It is unchanging and not an agent; its threefold application is difficult to perform.
Yet, because it yields fruit according to one's capacity, it is considered unfailing and desirable.
He who is independent of others and who realizes the sevenfold manifestation,
for whom there is fourfold reflection regarding form and so forth— his is considered equanimity.

In the path of omniscience, this path of seeing consists of the moments of the receptivities and knowledges of the knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge regarding the truths of suffering and so forth. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 3.11)
Form is neither permanent nor impermanent; it is utterly beyond extremes and pure.
It is unarisen and unceasing from the outset, resembling space and free from all defilement.
It is free from grasping and by its very nature beyond verbal expression;
for its meaning cannot be conveyed to others through speech.

The non-apprehension [of objects] brings about ultimate purity and the impossibility of disease; through the severance of the lower realms and the state of being beyond conceptualization, there is the direct realization of the fruit.
Non-association with signs regarding both the entity and its verbal expression,
and the non-arising of cognition— these are the moments of omniscience.
Thus, this very [perfection], again this very [perfection], indeed this very [perfection]—in these three ways, the completion of the three subjects has been fully elucidated. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 3.16)
The third chapter, on Omniscience, in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, a treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The definition of "aspects" (ākāra) is the modes of the knowledge of objects;
because there are three types of omniscience, they are considered to be of exactly three kinds.
Beginning with the aspect of non-existence and ending with the form of immovability,
these four aspects for each truth are recorded as fifteen on the path.
Regarding the cause, the path, suffering, and cessation,
they are proclaimed respectively as eight, seven, five, and sixteen.
Beginning with the foundations of mindfulness and ending with the aspects of Buddhahood,
these [thirty-seven factors] belong respectively to the disciples, the bodhisattvas, and the Buddhas.
These are considered to be thirty-seven, thirty-four, thirty, and nine, respectively,
according to the three types of omniscience, in accordance with the Truth of the Path.

Those who have performed services for the Buddhas, planted roots of merit under them, and are protected by virtuous friends, are the vessels for hearing this [Perfection of Wisdom]. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.6)
Through the practice of honoring the Buddhas, inquiring [about the Dharma], and [cultivating] generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth,
one is considered by the virtuous to be a fit vessel for receiving, retaining, and [mastering] the teachings.
Because they do not abide in form and the other [objects], because yoga with them is prohibited,
because their suchness is profound, and because they are difficult to fathom.

Because of the lack of authority in that [other vehicle], because of awakening only with great difficulty after a long time, regarding the prophecy, the state of non-retrogression, and the departure [from saṃsāra] together with its uninterruptedness; Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.9.
One is near to enlightenment and swift in the welfare of others because there is neither increase nor decrease;
and because there is no perception of dharma or non-dharma, nor of form, the inconceivable, and so forth.
It is non-conceptual regarding form and so forth, which are its objects and its nature;
it bestows the jewel of the fruit; it is pure, and it has a limit.
The fourteenfold quality consisting of the destruction of the Māras' power and so forth,
as well as the six faults, are to be understood together with the four sets of ten.
That by which something is characterized is to be known as the characteristic, and it is threefold:
knowledge, distinction, activity, and that intrinsic nature which is characterized. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.13)

Thus, regarding the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the world’s nature of being subject to dissolution, the mental activities of sentient beings, their contraction, and their outward wandering—(these are the objects of knowledge). Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.14.
And in the inexhaustible aspect, in the pervasive [knowledge] regarding those with passion and so forth, in the great and immeasurable, and in the invisible consciousness; (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.15)
Furthermore, the knowledge of the inconceivable consciousness is designated as "the opening of the eyes" and so forth;
beyond that is the knowledge of those [consciousnesses] by way of their suchness-aspect.
This exposition of the Sage’s awakening to suchness is, under the heading of omniscience, a summary of the characteristics of knowledge. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.17)
In emptiness, in the signless, and in that which is free from aspiration;
in non-arising, non-ceasing, and so forth, and in the unshakeable nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

In the context of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*), the characteristic of gnosis is held to consist in the absence of conceptual differentiation and the absence of characteristics regarding the unconditioned. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.19)

Relying upon their own specific duty, [one should practice] toward his dwelling, his honoring, his status as a teacher, the showing of respect, and the performance of worship toward him. // Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.20 //
Knowledge that possesses activity everywhere reveals the unseen;
it is the eye of knowledge that indicates and makes known the aspect of emptiness to the world.
The vision of inconceivable peace and the cessation of worldly perceptions is said to be the characteristic of gnosis in the system of the knowledge of all aspects.

The definition of the specific characteristics is set forth by six and ten moments, which are distinguished by specific qualities such as non-apprehension and have the truths as their objective domain.

Inconceivability, incomparability, the transcendence of the measurable and the countable, the inclusion of all noble ones, being cognizable by the wise, and uncommon knowledge. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.24)
Swift wisdom, the deficient and the complete, the practice and the attainment, the common object of focus, completeness, and full appropriation. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.25)
And the absence of relish should be known as the sixteenfold excellence, by which the path of excellence is distinguished from other paths. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.26)
It is the beneficial, the blissful, the protection, the refuge, the shelter, the ultimate resort, the island, and that which is designated as the guide for humanity.
Effortless, consisting in the non-realization of the fruits through the three vehicles—this is the final activity; such is the characteristic of activity.
The signs of the afflictions and their characteristics, the discordant factors and their remedies, seclusion, the difficult task, solitude, the objective, and non-apprehension.

That which is characterized by adherence to the prohibited, that which is designated as an objective support, that which is a misconception, and that which is non-obstructive—these are without going, coming, or birth. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.30)
The non-apprehension of suchness and its sixteenfold nature are perceived as if they were characteristics; this is considered the fourth characteristic.
Skill in the full realization of the gift of the signless and so forth is held to be conducive to liberation in this awakening to all aspects.

Faith has the Buddhas and so forth as its object; vigor has the sphere of giving and so forth as its domain; mindfulness is the perfection of intention; and meditative concentration is non-conceptuality.
Wisdom regarding all phenomena in all their aspects is called *prajñā*; it is fivefold.
Awakening is considered easy to realize for those with sharp faculties, but difficult to realize for those with dull faculties.
All sentient beings are the objective support for the stage of Heat (ūṣman) here;
the aspect [of practice], beginning with equanimity toward them, is taught as being tenfold.
For oneself, having desisted from evil and being established in giving and the like,
as well as enjoining others to those two and speaking their praises with a favorable disposition.

The Summits, the Patience based on oneself and others, and likewise the Knowledge of Truth, as well as the Supreme Mundane Dharmas, are to be understood by means of the ripening of sentient beings and so forth. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.37)
Those Bodhisattvas who, having attained the factors of penetration, abide on the paths of seeing and cultivation constitute here the group of those who are irreversible.
Through these twenty signs, such as the turning away from form and so forth,
which have been established, this is the characteristic of the non-retrogressive state for one abiding in the factors of penetration.

Turning away from form and the other [sense objects], the destruction of doubt and of moments [of unwholesome thought], one's own abiding in the wholesome, and the enjoining of others [to that same state]. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.40)
Generosity and the other perfections depend on others; lack of longing even for profound meanings;
friendliness; non-association with body and so forth; and the fivefold [non-association] with the obscurations. // Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.41 //
The abandonment of all latent tendencies, mindfulness, clear comprehension, purity,
and the non-arising of worms in one's robes and body.

Absence of crookedness in mind, undertaking of the ascetic practices (dhūta), freedom from envy and so forth, proceeding in accordance with the nature of reality (dharmatā), and seeking even in the hells for the sake of the world. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.43)

Not being led astray by others, [the recognition] that Māra is one who teaches other paths, and the realization that "this is Māra"—this is the conduct approved by the Buddhas. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.44)
Established in the stages of heat, summits, patiences, and the supreme mundane dharmas,
he does not turn back from perfect enlightenment by virtue of these twenty signs.
The moments of patience and knowledge— six, five, and five respectively—
in the path of seeing should be understood as the characteristics of the irreversible Bodhisattva.

The turning away from perceptions of form and so forth, firmness of mind in the two lower [vehicles], the cessation of those two vehicles, and the complete exhaustion of the factors of dhyāna and so forth.
Lightness of body and mind, skillful means in the enjoyment of desires, constant practice of celibacy, and purity of livelihood. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.48)

"Not" is used in relation to the aggregates and so forth, obstacles, the accumulations, that which begins with the sense faculties, battle, and stinginess and so forth; it is not used in relation to yoga and its application. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.49)
The negation of dwelling, the non-apprehension of even the subtlest dharma,
certainty in one's own stage, and abiding in the three stages.
The renunciation of life for the sake of the Dharma— these sixteen moments are the signs of non-retrogression for the wise one established on the path of seeing.
The path of cultivation is profound; its profundity consists of emptiness and so forth.
That profundity is the state of being free from the extremes of superimposition and denial.
Reflection, weighing, and profound contemplation constitute the path of cultivation;
they occur within the factors of penetration, on the path of seeing, and indeed on the path of cultivation itself.
This is accepted as being continuous, and it is ninefold in its modes,
through the further division of the weak, medium, and intense into [their own] weak and so forth.
Designations such as "incalculable" and so forth are not tenable from the perspective of ultimate truth;
they are accepted by the Sage only conventionally, as being the natural outflow of compassion.
Decrease and increase are not applicable to a reality that is beyond verbal expression.
What has been diminished by the path called "cultivation," and what has emerged? Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.56.
Just as awakening is, so too is this [attainment] the accomplisher of the desired goal;
awakening has the characteristic of suchness, and that [attainment] is likewise considered to have that same characteristic.
Awakening is not joined with the preceding mind, nor with the succeeding mind;
through the analogy of the lamp, the profound nature of phenomena is eightfold.
There is profundity in arising and in cessation, in suchness, in the object of knowledge, in giving, in conduct, and in non-dual skill in means. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 4.59)
Because all phenomena are like a dream, there is no conceptualization of existence or peace;
thus, the refutations of objections regarding the non-existence of karma and so forth are as previously explained.
Just as there is the purification of the world of sentient beings through the offering of that purification,
so too is there the purity of the Buddha-field, the receptacle-world.
Its object and its application are the transcendence of the enemies;
it is non-abiding, according to the piercing [of the target], and characterized by being uncommon.
Non-attachment, non-apprehension, being free from signs and aspirations,
the minor marks, and the immeasurables— skillful means are tenfold.
The Fourth Chapter: Complete Awakening to All Aspects, in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, a treatise on the instruction of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Even in dreams, the vision of all phenomena as appearing like a dream and so forth—
this is considered the twelvefold sign of yoga that has reached the summit.
Having made various analogies—beginning with the merit from worshipping as many Buddhas as there are beings born in Jambudvīpa—the increase consists of sixteen aspects. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.2)
The complete fulfillment of the dharmas of the three types of omniscience, which is unsurpassed and does not abandon the welfare of sentient beings, is designated as "establishment."

By means of the vastness of merit, this samādhi is proclaimed as being equal to a thousandfold world-system of four continents, a second-order intermediate thousandfold system, and a third-order great trichiliocosm.
In both engagement and withdrawal, each consists of nine aspects;
these conceptualizations of the apprehended and the apprehender are to be understood as having a nature that does not correspond to their objects.
The conceptualizations of a substantially existent being and a nominally existent being are considered to be the two types of subjects;
these two are each ninefold, according to the distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones.
If those two objects are not to be grasped in that manner, for whom could they be considered graspers?
Thus, their characteristic is emptiness by virtue of the state of being a grasper.

This [is the summary] regarding intrinsic nature and lineage, the practice and its full attainment, the object of knowledge and its non-delusion, and the counteractive factors and their opposites. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.8)

Regarding one's own realization, the agent, the action performed by that agent, and the fruit of that action—conceptualization based on the side of active engagement is considered to be ninefold. *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* 5.9.

Because it causes one to fall into the peace of existence, because of the deficiency in realization, because of the absence of spiritual support, and because of the impairment of the path; (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.10)
In being dependent on others for understanding, in turning back from the objective, in partiality, in diversity, and in delusion regarding the place and the departure; Abhs_5.11 //
And [the thought] regarding following behind— this ninefold conceptualization is based on the side of cessation and arises from the minds of the Śrāvakas and others.
The first should be known as the grasper, in the liberation from the grasped, in mental attention, and in the conjunction of the three elements. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.13)

Regarding the locus, adherence, and the designation of the entity of phenomena; regarding attachment and its antidote; and according to one's desire, and the destruction of rebirth. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.14)

Regarding the lack of departure according to the teaching, the determination of what is and is not the path, cessation along with origination, and the union with and separation from the objective basis; Abhs_5.15 //

When there is the station, the destruction of the lineage, the absence of aspiration and causes, and the perception of an adversary, there is another conceptualization which is the grasper. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.16)
The manifestation of others in enlightenment and the entrustment of its cause constitute the immediate cause for its attainment,
characterized by an abundance of merit.
Awakening is said to be the knowledge of the destruction and non-arising of the defilements;
for they [the defilements] are respectively absent from the objects of knowledge due to their destruction and non-arising. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.18)

When the fundamental nature (prakṛti) has not been ceased, is the collection of conceptual constructions exhausted by means of the path called "vision," or have they reached a state of non-arising? Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.19.

That the existence of phenomena and the destruction of obscurations regarding the objects of knowledge are spoken of by others as belonging to the Teacher—this is what causes me wonder. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.20)
Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added.
Reality is to be seen as it truly is; one who sees reality is liberated.
The mutual inclusion of each one of those [perfections] within giving and the others,
occurring in a single moment and subsumed by patience, is what is found here on the path of seeing.
Having entered that samādhi, he then contemplates dependent origination in the lion’s stretch— both in direct and reverse order.
Taking the consciousness belonging to the desire realm as its limit,
one proceeds through the two types of nine meditative attainments, including cessation, having entered and emerged from them while in a non-concentrated state.

By skipping over one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight [stages], there is a leap-entry meditation reaching as far as the cessation of perception and feeling; this is its incomparable nature.

Regarding the concise and the detailed, regarding being protected by the Buddhas and not being so protected, and regarding the absence of qualities in the three times— on this threefold path to the supreme good.
This first conceptualization of the apprehended object has the aspect of application as its sphere;
the second is considered the sphere of activity for the mind and mental factors.

The non-arising of the mind, lack of mental attention toward the seat of enlightenment, mental attention toward the Lesser Vehicle, and lack of mental attention toward perfect enlightenment [are the obstacles]. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.28)

On the path of cultivation, conceptual discrimination should be understood as being fourfold: that which consists in cultivation, that which consists in non-cultivation, its opposite, and that which is unreal. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.29)

The first type of grasper should be known as that which has the conceptual designation of a sentient being as its object; the second consists of the investigation of attachment regarding the non-emptiness of the conceptual designation of phenomena.
It is proclaimed [as an obstacle] regarding the performance of material things, the three vehicles, the impurity of offerings, and the corruption of conduct. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.31)
The other [object] is ninefold, consisting of the designation of the sentient being, its cause, and its object;
it is fully understood through the path of cultivation, as it is the adversary because it obstructs that [realization].
Regarding the three types of omniscience, [the obscurations] are respectively the threefold veils;
[they exist] regarding the path to peace, and regarding the conjunction with and disjunction from suchness and so forth.

The final conceptualization is considered to be the delusion regarding inequality, suffering, and so forth; regarding the nature of the afflictions; and regarding the absence of duality. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.34)
When these [three] hopes have perished, the excellences of qualities that accomplish the happiness of the world in all its aspects are, as it were, long-sighing. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.35)
All [perfections], by their collective effort, resort to that Great Being who possesses the desired fruit, just as rivers flow toward the great ocean.
Having established the inhabitants of the triple-thousandfold world system in the excellence of attaining the state of a disciple or a pratyekabuddha,
and having established them in the certainty of a bodhisattva, [the Buddha] taught the similes of virtue.
Having performed [these deeds], by virtue of the abundance of merit, immediately after the attainment of Buddhahood, there is the "uninterrupted" samādhi; and that is omniscience (sarvākārajñatā).
Its objective support is non-existence, and mindfulness is considered its dominant influence;
its aspect here is peace, for those who debate with the flow of verbal proliferation.

In the occurrence of the objective support, in the determination of its intrinsic nature, in the knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects, and in the ultimate as well as the conventional; Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.40.
In the application [of practice], regarding the Three Jewels, the means, the Sage’s timing, error, the correct path, and the antidote and its opposite; // Abhs_5.41 //

Regarding the characteristics and the cultivation [of the perfections], there are considered to be sixteen misconceptions concerning those who begin with the six and the ten, which serve as the support for the knowledge of all aspects.
The Fifth Chapter: The Culminating Clear Realization, in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, a Treatise of Instructions on the Perfection of Wisdom.
Through generosity, wisdom, and so forth up to the recollections of the Buddha and others,
and by means of the intrinsic nature of the non-existence of phenomena— this is considered the gradual practice.
The sixth chapter, on the Gradual Realization, in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, a treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Because all the outflow-free [dharmas] are subsumed even by each one individually,
this realization in a single moment by the Sage through giving and so forth is to be known.
Just as even a single small stone, when set in motion by men,
causes everything to shake all at once, so too does knowledge in a single moment.
When the state of the nature of maturation consists entirely of the pure,
then the perfection of wisdom arises as gnosis in a single moment.
Abiding in phenomena that are like a dream, one attains in a single moment the signlessness of all phenomena through the practice of giving and the other perfections.
One does not perceive the dream and the seer of that dream as a duality;
one perceives the non-dual reality of all phenomena in a single instant.
The seventh chapter, on the realization in a single moment, in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, a treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The essential body of the Sage is characterized by the nature of those untainted phenomena which have attained purity in all its aspects.
The factors conducive to enlightenment, the immeasurables, the liberations in their proper order, the ninefold meditative attainments, and the tenfold totalities. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.2)
The bases of mastery are of eight kinds according to their divisions;
[then there are] absence of conflict, knowledge resulting from prayer, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges.
Then there are the four purities in all their aspects and the ten masteries.
The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the absence of need for protection.
The threefold application of mindfulness, the threefold nature of non-confusion, the complete eradication of latent predispositions, and great compassion for living beings. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.5)
The eighteen unique qualities belonging exclusively to the Sage,
as well as the knowledge of all aspects— this is designated as the Dharma-body.

The Śrāvaka possesses the "non-affliction" (araṇā) because he has seen the truth; he avoids causing afflictions in others. The Victor’s non-affliction, however, exists in villages and other places for the purpose of cutting off the stream of those very afflictions.
Effortless, unattached, unimpeded, and ever-present;
that which dispels all questions is held to be the Buddha’s knowledge resulting from his vow.
Whenever and for whomever the cause has reached maturity,
that [Bodhisattva] manifests himself to perform whatever is beneficial for each of them.
For even when the rain-cloud pours down, a seed does not sprout;
likewise, even upon the appearance of Buddhas, one who lacks the capacity does not hear the auspicious [Dharma].
Thus, due to the vastness of his activity, the Buddha is described as all-pervading;
and because that very activity is inexhaustible, he is also said to be eternal.
This body of the Sage, consisting of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics,
is considered the enjoyment body (sāṃbhogika-kāya), because it enjoys the Mahāyāna.
His hands bear the mark of the wheel; his feet are like those of a tortoise; his fingers and toes are joined by a web;
his hands and feet are tender and supple; and his body is adorned with seven prominent parts. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.13)

He has long fingers, broad heels, and well-proportioned limbs; he is majestic, with straight limbs, feet like those of a conch, and body hair growing upward; he has shanks like those of an antelope, beautiful thighs and arms, and his private organ is sheathed within a sheath.

He is golden-colored and has delicate skin; his body hairs grow singly, each curling to the right; his face is marked by a tuft of hair (ūrṇā); his torso is like that of a lion; his shoulders are rounded and the space between them is well-filled.
His inferior taste is renowned as the best of tastes; his body is like a nyagrodha tree, equal in its circular proportions;
he has a crown protrusion on his head, broad and beautiful tongues, the voice of Brahmā, a jaw like that of a lion, and perfectly white [teeth].
The teeth are equal in size, closely set, and four sets of ten in number;
his eyes are dark blue with eyelashes like those of a bull—these indeed are the thirty-two marks.
Whichever cause there may be here that establishes each respective characteristic, this [path] fulfills that very cause; such is its characteristic of complete attainment.
Following after the gurus and so forth, firmness regarding the vow, gathering [disciples], attending upon them, and the giving of sublime things. // Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.19 //

The increase of the undertaking of releasing those condemned to death and the growth of the wholesome—such causes, as set forth in the sūtra, establish the [thirty-two] marks. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.20)
The nails and fingers of the Sage are copper-colored, glossy, and elevated;
they are rounded, well-defined, and tapering, while his veins are hidden and free of knots.
The ankles are hidden, the feet are even like those of a lion, an elephant, a brahmin, or a bull;
there is a courageous stride to the right, a graceful gait, and straightness of form.

Smoothness, regularity, purity, and softness [of the skin], the state of having pure limbs, the possession of full secondary marks, and the state of having a beautiful, broad, and well-proportioned body. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.23)
Evenness of stride, purity, delicateness of the eyes, lack of dejection, straightness of the limbs, and well-knit limbs; Abhisamaya 8.24.
Well-proportioned limbs, purity of light unobscured by darkness,
rounded, smooth, and slender bellies, and depth [of voice].
The navel spirals to the right and is beautiful to behold from all sides;
his conduct is pure, and his body is free from black moles.
The hands have scales that are soft, smooth, glossy, deep, and long-lined;
the mouth is not overly long, and the lips resemble the bimba fruit in their reflection.
The tongue is soft, slender, and red; his voice has the resonance of a thundercloud;
his speech is charming and pleasant; and his fangs are rounded, sharp, white, and even.
The nose is high, tapering, and supremely pure;
the eyes are wide, with lashes like those of a bull, and possess the appearance of lotus petals.
The eyebrows and the arms are long, smooth, very glossy, and have even hairs;
the ears are plump, long, symmetrical, and free from any defects.
The forehead is unmarred; the head is broad and full;
and the hair is the color of bees, curled, smooth, and not disheveled in form.
The hair of men is not coarse and carries away [all] fragrances;
the śrīvatsa and the svastika—these are considered the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) of a Buddha. Abhs_8.32 //
That by which the Sage performs diverse benefits for the world equally, until the end of existence, is the uninterrupted Emanation Body (nairmāṇika-kāya). (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.33)
Likewise, his karma is held to be uninterrupted until the end of saṃsāra;
it consists of the pacification of the realms of existence and the fourfold gathering [of beings]. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.34)

[The application of wisdom] is directed toward settling [beings] in that which is afflicted, in the realization of purification, in the true nature of the welfare of sentient beings, and in the six perfections. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.35)
In the Buddha-path, in emptiness by its very nature, in the cessation of duality, in conventional designation, in non-apprehension, and in the maturation of those who are inferior; Abhs_8.36.
In order to prevent attachment to the path of a bodhisattva,
for the attainment of awakening, and for the purification of the Buddha-field, [there is] determination.

In the immeasurable welfare of sentient beings, in qualities such as serving the Buddhas, in the factors of enlightenment, in the non-perishing of karmic actions, and in the vision of the truths; Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.38.
And in the abandonment of error, in the method of its lack of substantiality,
in purification together with its equipment, and in relation to the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The non-perception of differentiation and the establishment in discernment:
this is considered the twenty-sevenfold activity of the dharma-body.
The eighth chapter, on the Dharma-body, in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, a treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Its characteristics, its application, its excellence, its sequence, its culmination, and its maturation—this is another summary of the six topics. (1)
The object is threefold, the cause consists of four applications, and the result is the Dharmakāya along with its activity; this is another summary of the meaning in three parts. // 2 //
The treatise on the instruction of the Perfection of Wisdom entitled *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* is completed.
The work of the noble Maitreyanātha.
